I've written notes for vv. 25–41. I found almost nothing for **vv. 42–46** before the search tool hit its usage limit, and only a little on v. 47. No pages from Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal (ag.org, pneumareview), Orthodox or Bible Odyssey sites came up either. Following your rule, I've left those out rather than filling gaps from memory. Some Bible Hub and StudyLight pages show unlabeled commentary excerpts, so I name an author only where the page labels one.

---

## Acts 2:25–47: Research notes

**v. 25:**
- Peter sees that this Psalm speaks of David but also of someone greater, the Messiah. Guzik suggests Jesus may have taught Peter this when He opened the Scriptures to the disciples (Luke 24:44–45). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- Precept Austin says Psalm 16 is accepted by almost all authorities as a Messianic psalm and is probably the clearest Old Testament prediction of the Messiah's resurrection. It adds that Jewish tradition also applied the psalm to the Messiah. It quotes A.T. Robertson: the psalm has one speaker, and David's own experience is typical of (pictures) the Messiah's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary

**v. 26:**
- Precept Austin: "Therefore" points back to the benefits of setting the Lord always before oneself. "My body also will dwell in hope" expresses the Son of David's confidence that He could commit His body to the grave, sure that the Father would raise Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary
- On Psalm 16, Guzik says this "hope" is a settled confidence, not a mere wish, that life continues in God's presence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-16/

**v. 27:**
- *Traditional reading:* Jesus bore sin without becoming a sinner, so He remained the "Holy One" even in death. Because the Holy One could not be held by death, His resurrection was certain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- A Bible Hub Q&A page says "soul" (Hebrew *nephesh*) means the whole person. The parallel line about decay ties the promise to the body, so it means physical resurrection, not mere spiritual survival. Another Bible Hub page says Hades means the realm of the dead, not annihilation or hellfire: Jesus truly died but was not left there. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Acts_2_27_s_not_abandon_soul.htm ; https://biblehub.com/acts/2-31.htm
- *Where interpreters differ (Did Christ "descend into hell"?):*
  - **Ellicott:** Peter read this verse in light of 1 Peter 3:19. That reading lies behind the Apostles' Creed line "He descended into hell (Hades)": Christ's soul went to the world of the dead to carry on His redemptive work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-27.htm
  - **Barnes (Presbyterian):** The Creed's doctrine may have grown out of this verse. He says the Roman Catholic Church taught that Christ went to purgatory to free the spirits there. That is Barnes's description of Catholic teaching, not a Catholic source. He argues the verse says nothing about where Christ's soul went after death. "Soul" may simply mean "me," so the sense is "you will not leave me in the grave." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-27.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-27.html
  - **Matthew Poole:** Christ's soul was in paradise, as He promised the thief, so the verse probably means the grave could not hold His body long enough to decay. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-27.htm
  - **Calvin:** To leave the soul in hell means letting it be overwhelmed by destruction. Both Hebrew words used here mean the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-27.html
  - **Grudem**, quoted by Precept Austin, says the verse does not necessarily mean Christ entered hell; another meaning is possible. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary
  - **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** Hades is the state of the dead, Tartarus for the wicked and Elysium for the good. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-27.html
- *Other readings:* Meyer says the psalm's original meaning was "you won't let me die in my present danger." Constable calls it David's poetic way of saying God would not let him suffer ultimate humiliation; Peter then saw it fulfilled in Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-27.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-27.html

**v. 28:**
- JFB: "the paths of life" means resurrection life. "Full of joy in Your presence" means in glory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_002.cfm
- Guzik: instead of being punished for His work on the cross, Jesus was rewarded, as this verse describes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/

**v. 29:**
- David is dead and buried, so the psalm cannot be about him. It must speak of the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- Matthew Henry: David is called "patriarch" because he founded the royal family. Since his bones were still in the tomb, he must have spoken as a prophet about the Messiah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_002.cfm
- Barnes: nobody claimed David had risen. By honoring his tomb, the Jews themselves showed they believed his body had decayed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-29.html
- Poole: Peter calls them "brothers" to win a hearing as a fellow Jew. David's memory was greatly revered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-29.htm
- Precept Austin cites Nehemiah 3:16 for the tomb. Lenski, cited there, says that according to Dio Cassius the tomb fell into ruin under Hadrian (AD 133). https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary

**v. 30:**
- Precept Austin: Peter moves from David the patriarch to David the prophet. The verse alludes to Psalm 132:11 and 2 Samuel 7:12–13. John Phillips, quoted there, asks how a crucified Christ could sit on David's throne; the resurrection was part of the plan. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary
- Coffman: Jesus' exaltation fulfilled God's oath that a descendant of David would sit on his throne forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-33.html

**v. 31:**
- Robertson takes this as Peter's plain statement that David knew he was describing the Messiah's resurrection. The Precept Austin editor adds that, according to 1 Peter 1:10–12, prophets did not always fully understand what they wrote. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary

**v. 32:**
- Peter knew Jesus fulfilled the psalm because he had seen the risen Jesus himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- MacArthur sums up the argument: the psalm speaks of a resurrection. David did not rise, so it must speak of the Messiah. Jesus rose, so Jesus is the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary

**v. 33:**
- The crowd was seeing the work of the risen, ascended Jesus, who had sent His Spirit on the church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- NET Bible notes: "the right hand of God" stands for supreme power and authority and prepares for the Psalm 110 quotation. "The promise" is the Holy Spirit himself. "Poured out" picks up the verb from Joel in 2:17–18. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Act&chapter=2&verse=33
- *"By" or "to" the right hand?* Barnes and the Geneva notes read "by" God's right hand, meaning by His power. Meyer rejects "to" on grammatical grounds. Another note on the same page prefers "by" but says many scholars render "to." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-33.htm
- Calvin: Christ stands between God and us and hands on the gifts He received from the Father. The Spirit was given to believers before, but this fuller outpouring waited until Christ took His royal seat. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-33.html

**vv. 34–35:**
- Psalm 110:1 is quoted or alluded to at least 25 times in the New Testament, more than any other verse. Peter uses it to show that the Messiah is divine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- Calvin: David won many victories but never subdued all his enemies. Only Christ's kingdom fits the psalm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-34.html
- Barnes: David saw his descendant as also his Lord. Jesus used this same verse against the Pharisees (Matthew 22:42–46). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-34.html
- Bible.org: the outpouring of the Spirit was Israel's proof that Jesus had been exalted. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-110-what-do-you-think-about-christ

**v. 36:**
- Clarke: Jesus is not only Messiah but supreme Governor of everyone, Jews and Gentiles, angels and men. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-36.html
- JFB: proving Jesus was Messiah might have left hearts unchanged. Showing that the One they crucified was now Lord led them to mourn for "Him whom they had pierced." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_002.cfm
- Notes on the Bible Hub page:
  - "Lord" comes from Psalm 110 and "Christ" from the promise to David.
  - The Greek word order stresses the contrast: you crucified Him, but God made Him Lord and Christ.
  - To most of the hearers, "Jesus is the Christ" sounded foolish and "Jesus is Lord" sounded like blasphemy.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-36.htm

**v. 37:**
- Speaking in tongues produced only astonishment and mockery; conviction came only when the gospel was preached. In revival times, the sinner seeks out the evangelist instead of the other way round. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- Barnes: at this point the crowd was alarmed and afraid of punishment, which is not yet true repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-38.htm

**v. 38:**
- *Traditional reading:*
  - **Ellicott:** The apostles continue John the Baptist's call (repentance, washing, forgiveness), but baptism is now in Jesus' name and tied more closely to the gift of the Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-38.htm
  - **GotQuestions:** In Peter's sermon, repenting meant a change of mind about who Jesus is. https://www.gotquestions.org/repent-and-be-baptized.html
  - **Sam Storms:** "In the name of Jesus" means by His authority, and it is the believer's pledge of allegiance to Him. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/acts-2:38
  - One note on the Bible Hub page: naming Jesus does not leave out the Father and Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Jesus' name is stressed because these Jews had rejected Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-38.htm
- *Does baptism bring forgiveness? (the main dividing line):*
  - **Catholic:** Peter tells them to be baptized *in order to* receive forgiveness and the Spirit, which shows baptism is necessary for salvation. https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/necessity-of-baptism/acts238
  - **Coffman:** Faith, repentance and baptism are the terms of entry, and post-Reformation debates have not changed that. He criticizes readings that remove baptism from the human side of salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-38.html
  - **Reformed (Ligonier):** R.C. Sproul says baptism is a sign of forgiveness that does not automatically bring it; it must be joined with faith. Derek Thomas calls sacraments signs and seals of the gospel that point to Christ. https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/what-does-it-mean-that-baptism-is-for-the-forgiveness-of-sins
  - **Calvin:** Christ did not give "magical words," as he says the "Papists" imagine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-38.html
  - **GotQuestions:** The Greek *eis* ("for") can mean "because of," as in Matthew 12:41. "Repent" is plural, "be baptized" is singular, and "your sins" is plural again, so forgiveness goes with repenting. It also notes that Peter's next sermons promise forgiveness without mentioning baptism. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-Acts-2-38.html ; https://www.gotquestions.org/repent-and-be-baptized.html
  - **Sam Storms (charismatic):** He lists five views. He calls "because of" grammatically possible but "rare and unlikely," which is a direct disagreement with GotQuestions. His preferred view: the verse links baptism to repentance, as the outward expression of faith, and not to forgiveness. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/acts-2:38
  - **Bible Hub notes:** The water itself does not save, but refusing baptism would contradict real faith. https://biblehub.com/acts/2-38.htm
- *Other debates:*
  - **Constable (dispensationalist):** Peter did not require full submission to Christ's lordship here. This is a jab at "lordship salvation." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-38.html
  - ***What is "the gift of the Spirit"?*** "Contending for the Faith" says it is the indwelling Spirit himself (*dorea*, "gift"), not miraculous gifts (*charisma*). A Monergism article says receiving, being filled with and being baptized in the Spirit are one experience, not a second blessing after salvation, contrary to the view that believers still need a later Spirit-baptism. I found no Pentecostal source giving their own side. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-38.html ; https://www.monergism.com/baptism-spirit

**v. 39:**
- *Infant baptism (Reformed vs Baptist):*
  - **Ligonier:** Old-covenant promises and their sign (circumcision) included children, and Peter says the new-covenant promises are for believers' children too. About a quarter of New Testament baptisms are of whole households. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/infant-baptism
  - **Westminster Confession 28.4 (on Monergism)** cites these verses for baptizing the infants of believers. https://www.monergism.com/infant-baptism-covenantal-baptism-wcf-284
  - **Ligon Duncan (Presbyterian):** God attaches a sign to His promise to believers and their children, circumcision then and baptism now. **Justin Taylor (credobaptist)**, in the same post, replies that "you," "your children" and "those far off" stand on the same level, so the command to repent applies to all of them. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/justin-taylor/ligon-duncan-on-paedobaptism-and-some/
  - **A Bible Hub Q&A** argues against infant baptism: the commands are addressed to people able to respond, the "promise" is the Spirit, and the stress falls on God's calling, not on parents' faith. https://biblehub.com/q/Does_Acts_2_39_endorse_infant_baptism.htm
- *Catholic:* Peter did not limit baptism to adults, since the promise is "to your children." https://www.catholic.com/tract/infant-baptism:

**v. 40:**
- What Luke records is an inspired summary of a longer sermon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- Matthew Henry: once the word began to work, Peter kept pressing it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-41.html
- A note on the Bible Hub page says that turning to Christ means breaking with the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/2-38.htm

**v. 41:**
- The church grew from about 120 to about 3,120 in one day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
- MacArthur: the exact number suggests records were kept. Many Jewish ritual baths (*mikvahs*) have been found south of the temple mount, enough for mass baptisms. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-2-commentary
- Clarke: a Jew baptized in Jesus' name was cut off from his countrymen, so nobody did it without deep conviction. A note on the same page quotes F.F. Bruce: the New Testament never imagines an unbaptized Christian. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/2-41.html

**v. 47:**
- Guzik: their Christian life was daily, joyful and simple, a good example for us. The Lord's adding to the church was God's own pattern for growth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-2/
